t.6.12.1: Then Rāma, serene of spirit, having heard the son of Vāyu, the invincible and learned one replied with what was settled in his own heart.
t.6.12.3: One who has come to me in friendship I would never abandon in any way, even if there were some fault in him; this is not censured by the virtuous.
t.6.12.2: I too have something I wish to say concerning Vibhīṣaṇa. I want all of it to be heard by you, who are devoted to what is beneficial.
t.6.12.4: Having heard Rāma's words, Sugrīva, lord of the monkeys, moved by friendship, replied to Kākutstha.
t.6.12.5: What wonder is there in this, O knower of dharma, crest-jewel among the lords of the world, that you, being steadfast and established on the path of the good, should speak so nobly?
t.6.12.6: And this inner self of mine also knows Vibhīṣaṇa to be pure; he has been thoroughly examined on every side, both by inference and by his disposition.
t.6.12.7: Therefore, O Rāghava, let the greatly wise Vibhīṣaṇa quickly become an equal with us, and let him enter into friendship with us.
t.6.12.8: Having heard those words of Sugrīva and reflected upon them, Rāma then spoke still more auspicious words to that bull among monkeys.
t.6.12.9: Whether he be utterly wicked or not wicked, what of it? This night-roaming rākṣasa is in no way able to do me even the slightest harm.
t.6.12.10: Piśācas, Dānavas, Yakṣas, and the Rākṣasas upon the earth, all of them I could slay with the tip of my finger if I so wished, O lord of the monkey hosts.
t.6.12.11: For it is heard that an enemy who had come for refuge was honoured by a dove in due manner and invited to feast upon its own flesh.
t.6.12.13: Hear the most righteous verse sung long ago by Kaṇḍu, the supreme sage and speaker of truth, the son of the sage Kaṇva.
t.6.12.12: For even a dove received with hospitality the one who had come to him, the very abductor of his wife, O best of vānaras; how much more, then, should a person like me do so?
t.6.12.14: O scorcher of foes, for the sake of compassion one should not slay even an enemy who has come seeking refuge, wretched and pleading, with his hands joined in supplication.
t.6.12.15: Whether he is in distress or full of pride, an enemy who has come for refuge to his foes must be protected by one of disciplined mind, even at the cost of one's own life.
t.6.12.16: If he, out of fear, delusion, or even desire, does not protect him truly with his own strength, that is a sin condemned by the world.
t.6.12.17: If one who has come for refuge perishes unprotected while his protector looks on, he departs taking with him all the merit of that protector.
t.6.12.18: Thus great is the fault in failing to protect those who have sought refuge; it bars the way to heaven, brings infamy, and destroys strength and valour.
t.6.12.19: I shall indeed carry out the excellent words of Kaṇḍu just as they are meant; when their fruit comes forth, it will be most righteous, bringing glory and leading to heaven.
t.6.12.20: To one who has taken refuge in me even once and begs, saying, "I am yours," I grant freedom from fear of all beings; this is my vow.
t.6.12.21: Bring him here, O best of monkeys; I have granted him freedom from fear, O Sugrīva, whether he be Vibhīṣaṇa or Rāvaṇa himself.
t.6.12.22: Then, having heard those words of Sugrīva spoken by that lord of monkeys, the lord of men quickly went to meet Vibhīṣaṇa, as Puraṃdara went to meet the king of birds.
